name: Rabindranath Tagore
importanceReason: Tagore remade a Bengali literary language that had stiffened between Sanskrit tradition and English-style learning, forging a modern prose that could carry song, fiction, drama, and essay alike. The short stories he serialized in magazines through the 1890s created Bengali short fiction as a form in its own right, and through Rabindra Sangeet — which never separates poem from melody — he kept printed verse and orally transmitted song as a single body of work. His own English translation of Gitanjali, and the 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature it brought — the first awarded outside Europe — opened a channel through which non-Western literature could be read as literature rather than as folklore material. In the essay collection Nationalism, he criticized empire from the position of a colonial intellectual while at the same time questioning the nation-state as a form, charting a path on which anticolonial thought did not have to converge on nationalism.
readingEntryReason: It is short enough to read in one sitting, and because Tagore translated it into English himself, it is one of the rare cases where a reader can encounter the work with the least possible interference from a translator.
readingWarning: The most common path is to read only the English Gitanjali and file Tagore away as a 'sage of the East.' The English version turns the fixed meter of the Bengali verse into the tone of prose devotional prayer, so almost none of the original's rhythm or its layer of secular love poetry survives.
difficultyReason: The sentences and vocabulary are plain, but the novels ground characters' choices in the religious-reform debates of the Brahmo Samaj and in the Swadeshi movement, so without that background the direction of the conflicts is hard to follow.

name: Natsume Soseki
importanceReason: Soseki built a Japanese prose that could draw on classical Chinese learning and the spoken rhythms of rakugo at the same time, showing that genbun itchi — the unification of written and spoken language — could actually carry a novel, not just serve as a theory. Rather than the confessional mode of the shishosetsu, he treated egoism as it operates within relationships as his subject matter, translating the price that Meiji-imported modernity charged the individual into concrete situations such as love triangles and disputes over inheritance. When he left the university in 1907 to become a staff writer for the Asahi Shimbun, he made newspaper serialization the central form of publication in Japanese literature and opened a path by which a writer could establish authorship as a profession within journalism. Theory of Literature, which grew out of his unsuccessful period of study in London, was the first systematic attempt to explain how literature works without borrowing the standards of English literature.
readingEntryReason: It is a single volume with a clear three-part structure, and it compresses the central concerns of late Soseki — the end of the Meiji era and an individual's guilt — into one book.
readingWarning: Choosing I Am a Cat as a first book runs into trouble: its satire is dense with in-jokes from Meiji intellectual circles and allusions to classical Chinese texts, so without annotation a reader misses the points where it is funny and is left with only the length.
difficultyReason: The prose is plain, colloquial Japanese, but characters' choices are determined by institutions specific to the Meiji period — Imperial University pedigree, family inheritance, study abroad in the West — so without that background knowledge the conflicts can look trivial.

name: Lu Xun
importanceReason: Lu Xun proved with a single work, A Madman's Diary, that fiction could be written in the vernacular (baihua), abandoning the classical Chinese (wenyan) that had monopolized the right to write for two thousand years. He placed a classical-Chinese preface alongside a vernacular-Chinese body within the same piece, turning the very shift in language into an event within the work. In The True Story of Ah Q, he coined a diagnosis — the spiritual victory method, the trick of remembering defeat as victory — that made a fictional character into a common noun for a society's self-perception. The occasional essays (zawen) of his later years established the short polemical piece as a literary genre, and A Brief History of Chinese Fiction was the first work to organize vernacular narrative, long held in contempt, as an object of scholarship.
readingEntryReason: In barely a dozen pages, the double structure of a classical-Chinese preface and a vernacular diary is laid bare, so a single piece shows exactly what modern Chinese literature broke from in order to begin.
readingWarning: Starting with the zawen means reading without knowing the opponents and issues of the literary debates of 1920s–30s China, so irony that was precisely aimed can look like mere personal attack.
difficultyReason: The sentences are short and dry, but classical and vernacular Chinese alternate within a single work, and the targets of the irony are contemporary political and intellectual debates, so without annotation it is not visible what is being aimed at.

name: Ryūnosuke Akutagawa
importanceReason: Akutagawa took only the plot from classical tales such as the Konjaku Monogatarishu and grafted modern motive and doubt onto it, turning the historical story from a re-presentation of the past into a laboratory for cognition. In a Grove does nothing but line up mutually contradictory testimonies about a single murder and never renders a verdict, a construction that made the reliability of narration itself the novel's subject. In a Taisho literary world dominated by the shishosetsu, he kept pushing the tightly constructed short story to its limit, and the plotless-novel debate he waged with Tanizaki Jun'ichiro just before his death left that opposition on the record. The Akutagawa Prize, established in 1935, has kept his name as the gateway for new Japanese fiction ever since.
readingEntryReason: In barely ten pages, Akutagawa's method — stripping a classical tale down to its bare skeleton and replanting it with new motive — is present whole.
readingWarning: Approaching the story on the assumption that watching Kurosawa's film Rashomon amounts to having read it leads readers astray. The film was made by fusing the setting of Rashomon with the incident of In a Grove, so the two original stories are in fact separate works.
difficultyReason: Individual pieces are short and their incidents clear, so entry is easy, but most of them are twists on classical tales, and without knowing the source, the angle of the twist is invisible.

name: Yi Sang
importanceReason: Yi Sang treated the printed page itself, in colonial Gyeongseong, as the raw material of poetry. He pushed number tables, geometric figures, mirror-reversed type, and lines stripped of spacing directly into a newspaper's literary column, the first to demonstrate that Korean-language poetry could be an event of notation rather than a transmission of meaning. In his prose, the arrangement of an inert narrator supported by his wife recorded the economic and sexual incapacity of the colonial intellectual without explanation or allegory. His bilingual condition — working as a draftsman in the Government-General's architecture section and publishing poems first in a Japanese-language journal — shows that his experiments grew out of institutional and page-bound conditions rather than being imported from the Western avant-garde.
readingEntryReason: It runs the length of a single short story, and its structure — an opening aphorism set to work against the narrative that follows — makes Yi Sang's method easiest to recognize.
readingWarning: Starting with Ogamdo makes it easy to stall out hunting for the rule behind the number grids and mirror-image notation. It works better to first get a feel for his sentences through the prose pieces Wings and Gwontae before moving on to the poetry.
difficultyReason: Notation with spacing removed, a page layout in which numbers and figures stand in for lines of verse, and the bilingual layer of poems originally written in Japanese all overlap, so following the original text as it stands means enduring the formal experiment to the end.

name: Kim Sowol
importanceReason: Kim Sowol carried the three-beat meter and 7-5 syllable pattern of folk song into the free verse of the modern printed page, creating a method for rewriting the rhythm of songs a community used to sing into a single person's voice. Azaleas (1925) fixed the tone of a speaker enduring separation as the standard register of Korean lyric poetry, and Korean poetry after it defined its own place either by inheriting that register or by reacting against it. He is valued as well for using Pyongan-dialect vocabulary as poetic diction rather than as an exception to the standard language, and for formulating the principles of his own poetry himself in Sihon (1925).
readingEntryReason: It was the only poetry collection he published in his lifetime and is also his representative work, and it is short enough that a reader can take in the tone of the whole book at once, not just the title poem.
readingWarning: The most common misreading is to stop at the single poem Azaleas, read as a textbook poem of parting. Across the collection as a whole, wandering, a home that cannot be returned to, and a voice calling out to the dead occupy a far larger share.
difficultyReason: The vocabulary and syntax are plain and individual poems are short. Even so, a few passages of Pyongan dialect and archaic spelling trip up a reader without annotation.

name: Han Yong-un
importanceReason: Han Yong-un carried the paradoxical logic of Buddhism — that parting is itself meeting, that silence is itself speech — into the syntax of Korean honorific-register prose poetry. In Nimui Chimmuk (1926), the 'nim' addressed throughout is designed so that it never settles into any one of lover, Buddha, or a lost sovereignty, which let love song, religious utterance, and political utterance share the same sentence under censorship. That design cannot be separated from his own history: a monk who argued for institutional reform of Korean Buddhism in Joseon Bulgyo Yusinnon (1913), and a national representative among the signatories of the March 1st Declaration of Independence. Under conditions in which speech itself was blocked, making silence a form of speech became the very structure of the poetry.
readingEntryReason: Because it is a sequence bound into a single volume, it can be read straight through, and even reading only the opening poem and the preface-like Gunmal shows that 'nim' was designed never to settle into a single fixed referent.
readingWarning: A reading that substitutes 'the homeland' for 'nim' directly has long been in common circulation, but the collection itself never settles on that substitution. Fixing it to a single referent erases most of the shifts in tone that vary from poem to poem.
difficultyReason: The lines are long and the tone is a plain honorific register, but Buddhist terminology and paradoxical constructions that invert 'presence/absence' and 'meeting/parting' recur throughout, so a reader has to follow how the conclusion of one poem is overturned in the next.

name: Premchand
importanceReason: Premchand was a bilingual writer who began writing in Urdu and moved into Hindi, leaving the same stories in two versions of a Hindustani prose that was splitting into two separate writing systems. In place of the ornamental narrative of Persian-Urdu romance, he made rural economic facts — rent, debt, litigation — the events of his fiction, changing the very material Hindi fiction was made of. Godan (1936) narrates the bankruptcy of a peasant family not through statistics but through the time of the seasons and of debt, and it became the standard text of the Indian novel. In his 1936 presidential address to the founding conference of the All India Progressive Writers' Association, he defined literature not as entertainment but as a measure for judging reality, leaving behind the founding document of India's later leftist literature.
readingEntryReason: It is a short story of barely ten pages, and it most concisely sums up the cold-eyed gaze of his later work, presenting without comment a starving father and son who spend the money collected for a daughter-in-law's funeral shroud on drink.
readingWarning: Korean translations are scarce, so readers tend to approach him through English translations; because even a single work can diverge in title and text between its Hindi and Urdu versions, it is worth checking which version any given translation is based on.
difficultyReason: The prose and structure are plain realism, but the institutional vocabulary of the colonial countryside — tenancy, debt, caste, court procedure — drives the narrative, so without that background the scale of the conflicts does not register.
